payload.name: observer-controller
payload.scope: To implement state-space control when not all states are directly measurable, by combining a state estimator with a state-feedback law into a single dynamic compensator.

definition.body: observer-controller is a human-authored control design methodology that combines a state observer with a state-feedback controller, using the observer's estimated states as inputs to the feedback law so that a complete control system can be built when not all states are directly measurable. Parameters: (1) an observer (typically Luenberger or Kalman) that estimates the state vector from available measurements; (2) a feedback gain law (e.g. u = -Kx_hat) that drives the estimated states toward desired values; (3) the combined dynamics where the observer and controller eigenvalues are distinct and the control law acts on estimated rather than true states. definition.body: structured-singular-value is a human-authored mathematical measure that quantifies the worst-case effect of structured matrix uncertainty on closed-loop stability. payload.name: loop-shaping
payload.scope: To shape the loop gain frequency response across bandwidth so that closed-loop systems meet robustness and performance specifications through frequency-domain design.

definition.body: Loop-shaping is a human-authored frequency-domain control design methodology that shapes the loop gain magnitude and phase response across frequency to achieve desired closed-loop performance and robustness specifications. The construct maps the trade-off between sensitivity attenuation at low frequencies, disturbance rejection at mid-frequencies, and noise sensitivity at high frequencies, parameterized by crossover frequency, bandwidth, and roll-off rate. The persistence mechanism: maintained as a core design procedure in classical and modern control (Skogestad and Postlethwaite; Zhou, Doyle, and Glover), taught in all control engineering curricula, and implemented in MATLAB loop-shaping design tools and mu-synthesis workflows. It is distinct from pole-placement (time-domain eigenvalue assignment, not frequency shaping) and from LQR (optimal quadratic design, not heuristic frequency shaping). e.g.: shaping loop gain for an aircraft pitch channel to achieve 30 deg phase margin and 10 rad/s crossover; loop-shaping of a DC-DC converter to reject 100 Hz line ripple while limiting high-frequency noise gain; hard-disk-drive servo loop shaped to reject mechanical resonances above 1 kHz | not: pole-placement (time-domain eigenvalue assignment, not frequency-domain shaping); LQR (optimal quadratic cost minimization, not heuristic frequency shaping); root-locus (analytical method for visualizing pole migration with scalar gain variation, not a synthesis procedure) [formal: modelatio loopae | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: lmi
payload.scope: A convex constraint in robust control and optimization where a symmetric matrix, linear in decision variables, must be positive or negative semidefinite. Serves as the unifying computational framework for H-infinity control, pole placement, and robust stability analysis, replacing non-convex Riccati equations with tractable convex feasibility problems. Persisted in YALMPI, SeDuMi, Mosek, and SDPT4 solvers.

definition.body: A linear matrix inequality (LMI) is a convex constraint of the form F(x) = F₀ + x₁F₁ + ⋯ + xₙFₙ ≽ 0, where F₀, F₁, …, Fₙ are symmetric matrices of fixed dimension, x = (x₁, …, xₙ) are real decision variables, and ≽ 0 denotes positive semidefiniteness. The feasible set is the intersection of an affine subspace with the cone of positive semidefinite matrices, making LMI feasibility solvable in polynomial time via interior-point methods. Parameters: (1) the number of decision variables n, (2) the matrix dimension p×p, (3) the matrix coefficients F₀ through Fₙ. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic: LMI problems are encoded in convex optimization software (YALMPI, CVX, MOSEK) and solved as semidefinite programs (SDPs) across control synthesis, structural design, and operations research. e.g.: MATLAB's Robust Control Toolbox lmivar; YALMPI LMI model for H-infinity synthesis; CVX semidefinite program for robust state-feedback gain; SeDuMi solver for mixed sensitivity LMI | not: SDP; Lyapunov equation; scalar linear inequality [formal: inaequalitas matricialis linearis | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

definition.body: A Youla parametrization is a mathematical construction that parameterizes the set of all stabilizing controllers for a given linear time-invariant plant P. Given a plant P and a doubly coprime factorization P = NM⁻¹ = Ĩ⁻¹Ñ, every stabilizing controller C is expressed as C = (X + QD̃)(Ñ + MQ)⁻¹ where Q is an arbitrary stable transfer function (the Youla parameter), and X, D̃, Ñ, M are fixed stable factors from the coprime factorization. The parametrization persists through control theory textbooks and robust control software, where Q is optimized to meet performance and robustness specifications. e.g.: MATLAB Robust Control Toolbox youla function; Zhou-Doyle-Glover textbook parametrization; Python control library coprime factorization; Vidyasagar's Youla parametrization in H-infinity design | not: doubly coprime factorization; state-feedback; PID controller [formal: parametrizatio youla | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: lead-lag-compensator
payload.scope: To simultaneously improve a feedback system transient response and steady-state accuracy using a single compensator network with both phase-lead and phase-lag sections, parameterized by crossover frequency, phase-lag center frequency, and attenuation factors for each section.

definition.body: Lead-lag compensator is a human-made controller transfer function that combines a phase-lead section and a phase-lag section into a single compensator, enabling simultaneous improvement of transient response (via phase lead near crossover) and steady-state accuracy (via low-frequency gain boost from phase lag). Its standard form is C(s) = K(s/z_lead + 1)/(s/p_lead + 1) * (s/z_lag + 1)/(s/p_lag + 1) where p_lead > z_lead (phase-lead section) and p_lag < z_lag (phase-lag section). The lead section zero and pole are centered near the crossover frequency to add phase margin; the lag section zero and pole are centered well below crossover to boost low-frequency gain without significantly degrading phase margin. Parameters: (1) lead zero and pole locations setting phase-lead frequency and magnitude, (2) lag zero and pole locations setting phase-lag frequency and attenuation, (3) overall gain K. It is distinct from lead-compensator (phase lead only, no low-frequency gain boost), lag-compensator (low-frequency gain boost only, no phase lead), and PID-controller (different structure and tuning objectives). Persistence mechanism: maintained as a standard compensator design in classical control engineering — implemented in analog lead-lag networks, digital compensator sections, and tuning procedures in frequency-response design — encoded in Ogata Modern Control Engineering, Dorf and Smith Modern Control Engineering, and process control design practice. e.g.: lead-lag for DC motor speed control with 20 deg phase margin improvement; lead-lag compensator in aircraft pitch channel for transient and steady-state performance; compensator for DC-DC converter with lead at 1 kHz and lag at 100 Hz | not: lead-compensator (phase lead only, no lag section for low-frequency gain); lag-compensator (low-frequency gain boost only, no phase lead); cascaded lead-lag as two separate compensators in series, not a single network [formal: compensans principalis-retardans compositus | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]
